cards.headline: Israeli drone strikes kill at least seven Palestinians in central Gaza

pages.text: Israeli drone strikes killed at least seven Palestinians and wounded others in the central Gaza Strip, according to medical sources and Gaza's civil defense agency. These attacks occurred despite a ceasefire agreement that came into effect in October 2025. In the Bureij refugee camp in Deir el-Balah, medical sources told Al Jazeera that four Palestinians were killed when an Israeli drone struck the camp, with witnesses stating the drone targeted a group of civilians. Gaza's civil defense agency, a rescue force operating under Hamas authority, reported that one Palestinian was killed in a drone strike targeting a tent in the Al-Munasara camp for displaced people in Deir el-Balah, and another person was killed in a drone strike north of the Nuseirat refugee camp. Additionally, two Palestinians were killed when an Israeli drone struck civilians near the entrance to the city of Deir el-Balah. The Israeli military told AFP it had conducted several strikes targeting multiple military operatives in those locations. Al-Aqsa-Martyrs Hospital and Al-Awda Hospital each confirmed receiving two bodies following the strike southwest of Bureij refugee camp, while Al-Aqsa-Martyrs Hospital also confirmed receiving two bodies following the other strikes.

cards.headline: Approximately 170 dead pets found at dumping sites in Bulacan, Philippines

pages.text: Chris and Geraldine Taylor, who run the animal rescue NGO Luna and Furry Siblings (LAFS), say they have uncovered 15 dumping sites in the suburbs of Bulacan, near Manila, Philippines. In total, they have unearthed the remains of some 170 dead pets, including Belgian Malinois, golden retrievers, pugs, puppies, and cats. The remains were found in various locations, such as buried in vacant lots, floating in rivers, sealed in septic tanks, or dumped off service roads. Many of these animals are thought to have been sent to cremation businesses with the expectation they would be turned to ash, leading to concerns that grieving owners may not have received the service they paid for.

The discovery follows a Facebook livestream showing a man guiding a camera toward a cluster of plastic-wrapped objects spilling out of tall grass on a cracked back road. The man described the scene as a mass dumping, stating, “We have about 25 animals here that have been dumped in bags. A couple of cats, some dogs.” The packages in the video featured names such as Brandon, Ira, Lucky, and Sweet, along with numbers, including one marked 29kg (4.5 stone). Through the plastic, fur, claws, and a flattened ear were visible.

The situation has caused significant distress for pet owners. Revecca Calling, for example, expressed devastation after hearing about the found bodies, questioning if her dog, Olaf, was actually cremated.

cards.headline: Two Russian missiles and a drone crash in Poland during NATO military exercises

pages.text: Two Russian cruise missiles and a jet-powered drone crashed in south-eastern Poland on November 20, 2026, according to Polish officials. The incident occurred during Russian air attacks on Ukraine and coincided with major military exercises involving troops from 11 countries in a coalition known as the “coalition of the willing.” The crashes were reported in Nowy Lipowiec, Mołodycz, and Rudnik nad Sanem, locations situated between 30 miles (50km) and 60 miles from Nowa Dęba, where the military training is taking place. The incident occurred as the defence ministers of Britain, France, Estonia, Lithuania, and Poland were visiting the Nowa Dęba training site.

NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte described the incident as a “grave violation” of Polish airspace and stated on X that the development is “clearly dangerous” and a consequence of Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine. Rutte is expected to travel to Poland this weekend in response. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk called the incident an “intentional provocation” by Russia and noted that he had spoken with Rutte, who agreed that it “does not seem to be a coincidence” that the event took place the night before the drills. Poland’s defence minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, also stated he believed it was “not accidental” that the incident occurred on the same day as the joint military exercises.

European leaders have characterized the incident as an “irresponsible gamble” and a “provocation” that may further isolate Moscow and strengthen Western resolve to support Ukraine. Prime Minister Tusk indicated that the event suggests the coming months will pose “great challenges” for the region. The missile and drone crashes occurred amid a broader period of escalation; Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy reported that Russia fired more than 400 drones and over 110 missiles, including 27 ballistic missiles, in a massive assault that left at least nine dead and wounded more than two dozen people.

cards.headline: Saudi-led coalition intercepts three Houthi ballistic missiles targeting Riyadh

pages.text: The Saudi-led Coalition to Support Legitimacy in Yemen announced that air defenses intercepted and destroyed three ballistic missiles launched by Yemen’s Houthi militia toward Riyadh. The interceptions occurred shortly after 2 a.m., following a 1:53 a.m. Civil Defense alert warning Riyadh residents of an “aerial threat.” Witnesses in the capital reported hearing two explosions. The Houthis stated on X that they were striking targets across Saudi Arabia, including Riyadh. Following the interceptions, Civil Defense lifted the alert in Riyadh, stating the danger had passed. Civil Defense also issued early-warning alerts in the Al-Sulayyil governorate, south of Riyadh, and in Najran, near the border with Yemen.

The attack on Riyadh follows a wave of missile and drone activity across the Kingdom. On the evening of November 20, 2026, Saudi air defenses intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched toward the Jazan region. Debris from those missiles fell in the Al-Shuqaiq area, prompting an authority response. On that same date, the coalition reported intercepting five drones and three ballistic missiles, which included the two missiles aimed at Jazan. According to the coalition, four drones and another ballistic missile were intercepted over the Kingdom’s southern region, while a drone was shot down over the Riyadh region. Civil Defense warnings were also issued in the Jazan region and Khamis Mushayt in the Asir region as attacks continued.

In response to the hostilities, coalition spokesman Maj. Turki Al-Maliki stated that the coalition had targeted a main Houthi militia supply depot in Sanaa. Houthi-controlled Al-Masirah TV reported that Saudi Arabia carried out airstrikes on Yemen’s capital, Sanaa. Yemen has been in conflict since 2014, when the Houthis seized Sanaa and other provinces, leading a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in 2015 to support Yemen's government.

cards.headline: EU and UK agree to landmark deals on trade and youth mobility

pages.text: The United Kingdom and the European Union have reached agreements on trade and youth mobility during a summit in Brussels. UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham and European Union officials announced the deals, which leaders described as a significant step toward rebuilding ties a decade after Britain voted to leave the EU. The agreements include a youth experience project intended to increase opportunities for young people and a trade deal that European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen described as a “two way street” providing more choice for customers. Burnham called the arrangement a “landmark agreement” and stated it was intended to lift the life chances of young people, noting that Brexit had previously taken opportunities away from them.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen characterized the deals as a “turning point” in relations, stating the youth experience project would create lasting friendships. European Council President Antonio Costa said at a joint press conference that the EU respects the British decision to leave the bloc and respects the choice to strengthen ties in the post-Brexit era. Costa remarked that while the EU and UK may drive on opposite sides of the road, they are heading in the same direction. Burnham described the outcome as a “good day for Britain” and a “good day for Europe.”

cards.headline: Leaked news release announces Konrad Narth will lead Manitoba PCs into election before members vote

pages.text: Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew presented a leaked draft of a Progressive Conservative (PC) news release during question period, alleging the document announced interim leader Konrad Narth would lead the party into the next election before the party's executive council had voted on the matter. The news release, which was dated two days in advance, stated that the PC executive council had passed a motion endorsing Narth to remain in his role during the next provincial election campaign. The next provincial election is scheduled for Oct. 5, 2027, though it may be called sooner. Kinew described the document as a “charade” and an “absolute mockery,” alleging party leadership was overriding members by presupposing the outcome of an executive meeting that had not yet occurred. Narth, who was appointed interim leader in September following the resignation of Obby Khan, said he was “blindsided” that a confidential party document reached the premier. Narth stated he left question period early to investigate and found the party was preparing multiple news releases for various potential outcomes from the meeting. He suggested the premier may have accessed the files and chosen the most controversial version to release, adding that he has “serious concerns about the safety and protection of the party's files.”

The leaked news release included quotes from PC party president Peter Smith, stating the executive council was influenced by arguments that a rushed leadership race could lead members “to question the integrity of the process.” The release claimed that a leadership race would divert money, staff, and volunteer capacity away from the party's goal of winning the next election. The document stated, “We cannot hold a leadership race and prepare for a general election in the same year.”

cards.headline: Scientists investigate rare Bundibugyo Ebola virus amid rapid Democratic Republic of Congo outbreak

pages.text: Scientists and medics are working to understand the rare Bundibugyo version of the Ebola virus to explain its rapid spread and stop an outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). The virus is spreading at double the pace of the 2014-2016 Ebola outbreak in West Africa, which was the largest on record. According to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the epidemic toll includes 11,645 infections and 5,683 deaths. This is the 17th Ebola outbreak in the DRC, but it is the country's largest and fastest-growing. It took only 40 days after the crisis was declared in mid-May to surpass 1,000 confirmed cases, whereas the 2018 DRC Ebola outbreak took 235 days to reach that number. Currently, there are no licensed treatments or vaccines to fight the Bundibugyo virus, though Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, director of global health security Emanuele Capobianco stated that clinical trials of three Bundibugyo vaccines could lead to a breakthrough if security problems are resolved.

A key area of investigation involves Bundibugyo's symptoms, particularly in children, according to officials from the World Health Organization (WHO) and the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC). While Ebola infection can cause fever, vomiting, diarrhea, and severe internal or external bleeding, Yap Boum, Africa CDC’s deputy Ebola incident manager, said bleeding is occurring in only around 5 percent to 10 percent of confirmed cases in this outbreak. This makes bleeding less common than in outbreaks of the more prevalent Ebola species, Zaire. This symptom profile makes the disease easier to confuse with more common illnesses like malaria, which Boum said may have contributed to late detection. Additionally, tests designed for other Ebola species do not pick up Bundibugyo, creating early challenges with diagnosis and making it harder to track the spread as many people do not suspect Ebola and seek care.

Experts have cautioned against drawing early conclusions because data is limited, varied, and often difficult to collect. Daniel Bausch, a member of the WHO’s Ebola emergency committee and visiting professor at the Geneva Graduate Institute in Switzerland, noted that comparing different factors across or even within outbreaks is difficult. Furthermore, the outbreak's location in a part of eastern Congo already facing a humanitarian crisis could be complicating scientific findings. Catherine Smallwood, the WHO’s Ebola incident manager, said teams are gathering evidence to inform the response and expects to soon make statements regarding what is the same, what is different, and what needs to be adjusted. In response to the rising cases, neighboring Uganda has restricted cross-border travel and public gatherings in 34 high-risk districts bordering the DRC. Uganda has also forbidden certain concerts, festivals, and political rallies not cleared by the Ministry of Health, and required a 21-day quarantine or monitored self-isolation for travelers returning from the DRC.

cards.headline: Conflict in the Middle East hampers climate change efforts and causes environmental degradation

pages.text: Years of war across the Middle East have diverted resources, squeezed finances, and released tens of millions more tonnes of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere, according to officials, campaigners, experts, and academic documents reviewed by The National. While governments often possess the will to address the climate crisis, the UK-based charity Conflict and Environment Observatory stated in an October report that peace-building and conflict prevention should be viewed as a dimension of climate action due to the damage wars cause. Many regional governments have been forced to prioritize reconstruction and more urgent needs over climate mitigation. During the Cop31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, some conflict-stricken Middle Eastern states sought increased international support to reduce greenhouse gas emissions.

In the occupied West Bank and Gaza, Zaghloul Samhan, head of Palestine’s environment authority, described the situation as an ecocide alongside ongoing discussions regarding genocide. Samhan, who manages pollution, waste, and the climate crisis in these areas, told The National that three years of conflict have ravaged the land, air, and water. The United Nations has stated that the scale of environmental degradation in the Gaza enclave is “immense,” noting that nearly all of its crops, trees, and grassland have been damaged. Samhan noted that a war-worsened financial crisis prevents the state from initiating large-scale projects to mitigate climate impacts, such as water scarcity, lower rainfall, and rising temperatures. In the West Bank, the World Bank reported in May that while solar power generation has increased, scaling the supply would require approximately $1.5 billion for electricity generation investment and another $330 million for network upgrades.

Lebanon is also seeking international assistance to manage shifting environmental priorities. Lebanon’s Environment Minister, Tamara El Zein, told The National that the country's delegation is seeking accelerated access to international climate funds because national priorities shift from one year to another. This request comes as negotiations at the annual climate summit enter their final hours.

cards.headline: French Senate approves law granting police a presumption of legitimate self-defense

pages.text: The French Senate has given final approval to legislation that grants police officers a presumption of legitimate self-defense when using firearms. The right-leaning Senate approved the text with 205 votes to 110, following a lower house vote in July. On November 19, 2026, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez stated the law would end the automatic practice of taking a police officer or gendarme into custody after they use their weapon, aiming to correct the reflex of systematically questioning the work of security forces. The law stipulates that when officers use their weapons, they are presumed to have acted within the framework of the law. Supporters of the bill include the government and the party of far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen, who argue the measure is necessary to prevent officers from being automatically suspected of using disproportionate force.

Critics and activists have slammed the legislation, with some labeling it a “licence to kill.” The Human Rights League argued the law will block the opening of investigations in specific scenarios, such as a police shooting following a failure to comply with a traffic stop or during crowd control at protests. Activists contend the law will hamper investigations and make holding security forces accountable more difficult in a country where alleged police brutality cases rarely reach a criminal court. This legislative development follows weeks of student-led protests that brought the issue of police brutality back into public focus. Left-wing lawmakers have vowed to challenge the bill before France's Constitutional Council, the country's highest constitutional authority, in an attempt to halt the bill from becoming law. The debate occurs alongside reports from France's rights chief stating that young men perceived as Arab, Black, or from North Africa are four times more likely to be stopped than the rest of the population.

cards.headline: Indian man sentenced to more than 19 years for conspiring to kill Sikh separatist in New York

pages.text: Nikhil Gupta, 55, was sentenced to 235 months in prison by a Manhattan federal court judge after admitting to orchestrating a failed plot to murder Gurpatwant Singh Pannun. Pannun is a dual U.S.-Canadian citizen and a lawyer for Sikhs for Justice, an organization that advocates for a sovereign Sikh state in northern India known as Khalistan. U.S. and Canadian authorities have characterized the plot as part of a broader effort by the Indian government to target Indian dissidents. While India's government has denied involvement and stated such plots are against government policy, prosecutors accused Gupta of working with an Indian government official to hire a hitman for the assassination. The discovery of these alleged plots has tested diplomatic relations between India and North American nations. This follows a wave of violence targeting Sikh separatists, including the June 2023 fatal shooting of Hardeep Singh Nijjar in Surrey, B.C., an event for which then-prime minister Justin Trudeau accused agents of the Indian government of involvement, a claim New Delhi denied.

Gupta pleaded guilty in February to murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire, and conspiracy to commit money laundering. According to court papers, an Indian foreign intelligence service official, Vikash Yadav, recruited Gupta in May 2023 to orchestrate the assassination of Pannun. Gupta and Yadav arranged to have $15,000 in U.S. cash delivered to a purported hitman, who was actually an undercover U.S. law enforcement officer. Court documents also indicate that Yadav arranged through dealings brokered by Gupta to pay $100,000 U.S. to the purported hitman. Gupta has been jailed in Brooklyn since his June 2024 extradition from the Czech Republic, where he had been arrested a year earlier. Yadav is also charged in the case but is not in U.S. custody, and it is unclear if he has hired a defense lawyer. Prosecutors from the Manhattan U.S. attorney’s office had recommended a sentence of approximately 24 years. During the hearing, prosecutor Ashley Nicolas stated, “This case cuts to the very core of American values. We don’t condone the use of violence to silence voices in this country, ever.” Addressing the court, Gupta said he regretted straying from the non-violent example set by Indian independence leader Mahatma Gandhi.

cards.headline: International Court of Justice rules Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya minority

pages.text: The International Court of Justice (ICJ), the United Nations' top court, has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against its Muslim Rohingya minority. The decision recognizes that the Myanmar military intentionally attempted to destroy the group through a campaign of mass killings and rape in 2017. This ruling follows years of legal efforts by the Rohingya to seek international recognition of the atrocities committed against them.

The 2017 crackdown in Myanmar resulted in more than 10,000 Rohingya killed and forced approximately 700,000 people to flee to neighboring Bangladesh. Other reports indicate that nearly one million Rohingya were forced to flee to Bangladesh during that period. Following the ruling in The Hague, Netherlands, Rohingya community members expressed relief, with some reporting tears in the courtroom and others celebrating in refugee camps in Bangladesh.

While the ruling provides legal vindication, the subsequent actions required to address the genocide remain in the hands of governments around the world. Observers have noted that the ruling against Myanmar may have implications for legal proceedings regarding Israel’s actions in Gaza.

cards.headline: Anthropic sets record US$81 billion IPO on Nasdaq

pages.text: Anthropic, the artificial intelligence company behind Claude, has completed the largest initial public offering (IPO) in history. By listing on the Nasdaq stock market, the company raised US$81 billion, surpassing the previous record of US$75 billion held by SpaceX. Anthropic's share price, which was initially set at US$83, rose to US$111 following its debut. This surge briefly pushed the company's valuation above US$2 trillion before the price fell as investors took profits.

The successful listing occurs during a period of uncertainty for the artificial intelligence sector. Investors are increasingly questioning if the massive capital being invested in the AI boom is justified, leading many to reduce their exposure to technology stocks. This instability follows the departure of Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang following an affair scandal. While Anthropic's debut establishes a benchmark for rival OpenAI, which still plans to go public, the result may reflect demand for Anthropic specifically rather than a broad vote of confidence in the global AI industry. At the end of October, Anthropic's annualised revenue run rate—an estimate of yearly revenue based on the previous month's performance—was US$81 billion.

cards.headline: Russian missile and drone strikes hit Ukraine, killing at least eight people

pages.text: Russia launched a massive overnight assault on Ukraine involving approximately 400 drones and over 110 missiles, targeting nine regions including the capital, Kyiv. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described the operation as one of the most massive strikes of the war so far. The attack resulted in at least eight deaths and nearly 30 injuries, according to Zelenskyy, though other reports cited at least nine dead and 28 injured. In the western city of Lviv, Mayor Andriy Sadovyi reported that two people were killed in a strike on the Sknyliv railway station, specifically hitting the station's ticket terminal. In Kyiv, authorities confirmed six deaths, with six of the total reported deaths occurring in the capital. Prime Minister Serhiy Koretsky stated that 28 people were injured, noting that an ambulance hospital in Kharkiv was among the targets. Ukrainian air force communications head Yuriy Ignat called the assault one of the most powerful attacks since the 2022 invasion began.

The strikes targeted civilian infrastructure, including hospitals, residential and commercial buildings, and essential services. In Kyiv, ballistic missiles hit three bridges spanning the Dnipro River: the Podilsko-Voskresensky Bridge, the Darnytskyi Bridge, and the Southern Bridge. These vital routes have been closed to traffic, causing significant disruption. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko urged residents to avoid traveling into the city by private car unless absolutely necessary, noting that an unspecified critical infrastructure facility was damaged and seven medical personnel were injured. The barrage followed an earlier wave of attacks that damaged diplomatic premises in Kyiv. The Russian strikes come days after Ukraine damaged the strategically important Crimean Bridge, a link built by the Kremlin to connect Russia to the occupied Crimean peninsula. Russian President Vladimir Putin had previously threatened a 'painful' retaliation for the damage to that bridge.

The aerial attacks also impacted Poland, a NATO member. Polish Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz confirmed three violations of Polish airspace after two Russian cruise missiles and a jet-powered drone crashed in the south-eastern areas of Nowy Lipowiec, Mołodycz, and Rudnik nad Sanem. These locations are between 30 and 60 miles from Nowa Dęba, where major western military exercises involving troops from 11 countries, including the UK, are taking place. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk called the incident an 'intentional provocation' by Moscow, stating it did not seem to be a coincidence that the strikes occurred the night before the drills. Tusk noted he had spoken with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte regarding the incident. The strikes coincided with a period of international discussions regarding the war and Kremlin opposition to US claims that Russia might be open to Western-backed security guarantees for Ukraine.

cards.headline: European leaders express readiness for negotiations with Russia to end war in Ukraine

pages.text: European leaders have stated they are prepared to negotiate with Russia to end the war in Ukraine, signaling a united position in support of Kyiv. Speaking at a summit of Ukraine's allies, known as the Coalition of the Willing, in Berlin, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Europe maintains a clear, consistent, and united negotiating position. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz added that Moscow's demands are not realistic and suggested that new talks involving European leaders could occur soon on neutral ground, such as the United Arab Emirates. Merz noted that Germany, France, the UK, Poland, and Italy would represent European interests during such discussions.

cards.headline: World Food Programme requires $12.1 billion to assist 91 million people in 2027

pages.text: The World Food Programme (WFP) will require $12.1 billion to assist 91 million people in 2027, according to the agency's Global Outlook for 2027. Assistant Executive Director Matthew Hollingworth warned that millions more will go hungry as funding shortfalls continue and another global food crisis looms. The report reveals that at least 266 million people worldwide face acute hunger, with roughly 39 million at emergency levels or worse. Hollingworth, speaking to journalists in Geneva and from headquarters in Rome, stated that the agency will continue to reach the most displaced and vulnerable people who are starving each day.

WFP officials noted that aid budgets are being slashed, forcing the agency to prioritize only the most critical cases. Hollingworth said teams are making difficult decisions on the ground that inevitably mean leaving people behind, adding that the gap between those the agency can and cannot reach is likely to grow larger. The agency called for flexible, predictable funding to allow resources to be directed to areas with the greatest needs to ensure maximum impact for every dollar.

Several factors are driving food insecurity, including conflict, economic shocks, and climate change. Hollingworth highlighted that conflict has created triple choke points at three crucial shipping lanes: the Strait of Hormuz, the Bab al-Mandab Strait, and the Black Sea. Additionally, the Super El Niño climate pattern is disrupting harvests while rising fuel and transport costs impact food prices. Hollingworth warned that the world could soon face a third global food crisis in six years, following the impacts of COVID and the war in Ukraine.

cards.headline: US military warns of force against vessels using ship-to-ship transfers to bypass Iran blockade

pages.text: The United States military has tightened its naval blockade of Iran, warning that vessels receiving Iranian cargo through ship-to-ship transfers will face military action. In an advisory issued on November 18, 2026, US Central Command (CENTCOM) stated that any ship receiving cargo via a transfer from a vessel carrying cargo loaded at an Iranian port or along the country's coastline could be considered to be “evading the blockade.” This applies even if the receiving ship has not entered Iranian ports or approached the Iranian coastline. CENTCOM warned that such ships may be stopped, boarded, diverted, captured, or directed to proceed to the Iranian port where the cargo originated, and that failure to comply with orders could result in the use of force. This move aims to close a loophole that has allowed some Iranian petroleum products to reach international markets despite a Washington-led blockade of Iranian ports and oil exports that has been in place since mid-July.

The tightening of the blockade comes as Tehran seeks to revive its oil exports. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has repeatedly warned of retaliation against attacks on Iranian vessels. While analysts suggest Iran is unlikely to break the blockade through military means, they note Tehran could attempt to make enforcement politically and economically costly for Washington, which raises the risk of a wider regional confrontation in the Middle East. Andreas Krieg, an associate professor in Security Studies at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera that the situation is “potentially one of the most dangerous escalation scenarios we have seen in recent weeks.”

cards.headline: Al Sharpton calls for unity following killing of 15-year-old Ghanaian teenager Javits

pages.text: American civil rights activist Rev. Al Sharpton has called on African American and immigrant communities to confront hatred and divisions among young people following the killing of 15-year-old Ghanaian Badu Nkansah Frimpong, popularly known as Javits. Delivering the eulogy at Javits’ funeral in the Bronx, New York, on Friday, November 20, 2026, Sharpton said the teenager's death should serve as a wake-up call for communities to address hostility, particularly between people of African descent. While Sharpton acknowledged that the full circumstances surrounding Javits’ death had not been established, he insisted that the consequences of the violence require a collective response.

Sharpton expressed concern that tensions between some African Americans and African immigrants, including prejudice against people with different accents and backgrounds, are influencing younger generations. He described this as a ``poison'' that has affected children and urged both communities to recognize their shared heritage and stand together against violence. During the service, Sharpton also noted he was troubled by the limited presence of some African American community members at the funeral, arguing that the killing should concern everyone regardless of the identities of those involved. He challenged parents to use family gatherings, such as Thanksgiving celebrations, to teach children tolerance, respect, and love for people from different backgrounds.

cards.headline: Froglife awarded nearly £890,000 to restore freshwater habitats at former Yorkshire colliery sites

pages.text: The charity Froglife has been awarded £889,761 from The National Lottery Heritage Fund for its Coalface to Wildspace project. The initiative aims to create and restore habitats for amphibians and lizards at two former colliery sites in South Yorkshire, specifically in Rother Valley, as well as at other locations in North and West Yorkshire. The project will focus on Dinnington Woodland, which was originally regenerated through the National Coalfields Programme after the pits there closed in the 1990s, and Kiveton and Dinnington Community Woodlands. Across Yorkshire, the project intends to create 48 new ponds, improve 93 existing freshwater habitats, and establish new “neighbourhood wildlife corridors” using small ponds and bug hotels. These corridors are designed to act as stepping stones for wildlife ranging from insects to birds, providing food, shelter, and water to improve biodiversity and help animals move between habitats across former industrial sites.

The Coalface to Wildspace project is funded for the next four years. Froglife has previously conducted similar projects in Scotland and the Midlands. Sheila Grundry of Froglife stated that the addition of freshwater would make a lasting difference for frogs and other wildlife while providing local people with opportunities to learn new skills. Project manager in Yorkshire, conservationist Andy Goff, said the transformation is intended for everyone and expressed interest in involving people from across Yorkshire to engage with local nature. Rother Valley MP Jake Richards described the project as important for the area.

cards.headline: Five children die with measles-like symptoms in Bangladesh

pages.text: Five more children died with measles-like symptoms in Bangladesh during a 24-hour period ending at 8:00 am on November 20, 2026, according to a Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) press release. During that same period, 1,270 suspected and confirmed measles cases were reported. No deaths from confirmed measles were reported in the last 24 hours. Since March 15, 2026, the total number of deaths from suspected measles has reached 1,236, while the total number of deaths from confirmed measles since that date is 105. The combined total of fatalities from confirmed measles and measles-like symptoms has reached 1,341 since March 15, 2026.

In the 24-hour period ending at 8:00 am on November 20, 2026, there were 1,185 reported suspected measles cases and 85 confirmed measles cases. Since March 15, 2026, the number of suspected measles cases has reached 254,593, and the number of confirmed measles cases has reached 25,966. Between March 15, 2026, and November 20, 2026, a total of 227,675 patients with suspected measles were admitted to various hospitals across the country, and 218,910 patients were discharged.

cards.headline: Excitons in atom-thin materials mimic light particles, confirming a decade-old prediction

pages.text: Researchers at Yale have observed energy-carrying composite particles called excitons moving in an unexpected way within two-dimensional (2D) materials. This observation confirms a prediction made ten years ago by Diana Qiu, an assistant professor of materials science, that excitons in materials thinned to a few atomic layers would act more like light particles, or photons. In these 2D materials, the energy of the excitons is in direct proportion to their momentum, a behavior characteristic of light. This finding, published in Nature Physics, could influence the development of quantum technologies, LEDs, solar energy, and other optoelectronic technologies.

Excitons are formed when light shines on a material, exciting an electron and causing it to move away from the atom's nucleus. This movement leaves behind a vacancy known as a hole, which acts as a particle itself due to quantum mechanics. The negatively charged electron and the positively charged hole attract one another to form a bound pair, known as an exciton. Understanding how these excitons move through a material is necessary for determining the expected energy or current produced by photovoltaic devices, such as next-generation solar cells.

cards.headline: President Mahama commissions national DNA laboratory in Ghana

pages.text: President John Mahama has commissioned a national Human Identification Laboratory at the Noguchi Memorial Institute for Medical Research to increase Ghana's capacity for DNA testing. The facility, known as the DNA Laboratory, is intended to support criminal investigations, the identification of disaster victims, and the resolution of disputed family relationships, such as paternity, maternity, and inheritance cases. By providing local testing services, the laboratory aims to reduce the country's reliance on foreign laboratories for specialized forensic analysis.

President Mahama stated the investment addresses a gap in Ghana's forensic and emergency response systems. He cited an August 2025 helicopter crash that killed eight people, noting that Ghana had to transport tissue samples to South Africa for DNA analysis. This process resulted in families waiting several days to identify relatives, an experience the President described as a moment of shame for the country. The new facility is intended to allow Ghana to handle similar incidents more quickly and independently while strengthening the resolution of complex criminal cases.

Health Minister Kwabena Mintah Akandoh said the laboratory was established following a presidential directive after the helicopter disaster. He explained that while Ghana possesses qualified scientists capable of conducting DNA analysis, the country previously lacked the specialized equipment required to perform the tests locally. Alongside the DNA laboratory, the President also commissioned new vaccine research and development laboratories to build local capacity for vaccine production, with the first vaccines bottled in Ghana expected to be on the market in 2027.

cards.headline: Black market thrives as a result of siege on Yemen's Taiz

pages.text: A black market for essential goods has emerged in Taiz, Yemen, as the city faces a siege that has cut off supplies and caused prices to skyrocket. Since October, the Iran-backed Houthis have tightened their grip on the western city, separating it from Aden, the interim seat of the internationally recognised government. While the Houthis deny preventing food and medical supplies from reaching the city, residents report shortages of fuel, gas, and food items such as tomatoes and onions. Taiz resident Hamoud Bajash described the situation by saying, “We are besieged, three million people inside a prison,” and noted that lives have become dependent on the black market.

cards.headline: ALMA observations reveal a giant gas ring and budding hourglass nebula around star IRAS 06530-0213

pages.text: Astronomers using the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) have captured images of a star in transition, revealing a giant ring of gas and an hourglass-shaped nebula forming around the star IRAS 06530-0213. Located approximately 12,000 light-years away in the constellation Monoceros, the star is undergoing a brief and violent transformation from a bloated red giant into a glowing planetary nebula—a sculpted cloud of gas left behind when a star sheds its outer layers. This transition is thought to take only a few thousand years, making such observations rare. The newly imaged gas ring appears to be a fossil of the star's last thermonuclear flare-up, encircling the hourglass nebula that is currently taking shape.

The study, led by astronomers at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) and published in The Astrophysical Journal, provides a snapshot of a process called a thermal pulse. Late in its life, a star like IRAS 06530-0213 burns hydrogen and helium in shells around its core. During a thermal pulse, the helium shell undergoes a brief burst of nuclear burning that jolts the star and flings material into space. While theorists have long predicted that these pulses leave behind shells of gas, and similar shells have been seen around other aging stars, researchers had not previously observed one around a star that had already begun its final transformation into a planetary nebula. Raghvendra Sahai, a senior research scientist at JPL and lead author of the study, described the images as a real-time snapshot of the star's death throes.

cards.headline: Report finds higher rates of chronic conditions and early death in northern Ontario First Nations

pages.text: Northern Ontario First Nations communities face significantly higher rates of chronic disorders and early death compared to the rest of Ontario, according to a report released in Thunder Bay by Mamow Ahyamowen. The alliance, which consists of 11 First Nations health and social service agencies, released the report titled “Reclaiming Our Health: Exploring Chronic Conditions in Participating Northern Ontario First Nations.” It found that approximately 61 per cent of band members were dying before retirement age, compared to 22 per cent for Ontario overall. The report analyzed 22 chronic conditions among members of 70 First Nations between 2003 and 2022, comparing their prevalence to provincial averages.

The study identified several specific health disparities. For northern Ontario First Nations, rates of rheumatoid arthritis were 14.4 times higher, chronic pancreatitis were 4.7 times higher, and substance use disorder were 4.3 times higher than the provincial average. Maureen Gustafson, a knowledge translation and exchange specialist for Mamow Ahyamowen, stated that the report's long-term scope allows for a longitudinal understanding of health challenges by observing trends and patterns over time. Mamow Ahyamowen was formed a decade ago to provide health-care data to First Nations that have historically struggled to obtain such information, with Gustafson noting that the goal is to return data to communities that has often been held by non-Indigenous organizations and institutions.

Alvin Fiddler, Grand Chief of Nishnawbe Aski Nation (NAN)—an organization representing 49 First Nations across Treaties 9 and 5 that was not involved in creating the report—said the findings reaffirm or validate what has been heard from communities. The data highlights ongoing health inequities in the region, specifically regarding the prevalence of chronic illnesses and mortality rates among northern Ontario First Nations members.

cards.headline: Syrian photographer recovers personal archive in Raqqa after more than a decade

pages.text: Ahmed al-Bekkar, a 66-year-old Syrian photographer, has recovered his personal archive in the northern city of Raqqa by tearing down a wall he built to conceal his library entrance. Bekkar had sealed off the library to protect his books, photographs, and personal documents before fleeing Syria due to war, looting, and attacks by the Daesh (ISIS) terrorist group and forces of Syria's now-ousted regime. After spending 10 years in Istanbul, Türkiye, Bekkar returned to Raqqa to reclaim the space, which he described to Anadolu as a way of reconnecting with his childhood, youth, and lost family members.

During his decade in Türkiye, Bekkar maintained his artistic career and helped establish the House of Migrants association and the Turkish-Arab Art House. He held two solo exhibitions in Istanbul's Fatih district: a first exhibition titled “Memories of My Homeland,” which documented Raqqa, other parts of Syria, and war-related destruction, and a second titled “Istanbul, Farewell,” which showcased the architecture and natural beauty of the city that hosted him. Since returning to Raqqa, Bekkar has been revisiting historical sites he previously photographed to document their current condition.

cards.headline: Protests erupt at Al-Qadisiyah University in southern Iraq after removal of male professors teaching women

pages.text: Female students at Al-Qadisiyah University in southern Iraq have held protests for approximately two weeks following the university's decision to remove male professors from teaching female students. An estimated as many as 400 women have joined the demonstrations, calling for the return of the professors. Activists have criticized the move, describing it as a policy of gender segregation similar to that of the Taliban. The university stated the decision was intended to “prevent the mixing” of men and women and claimed the change was requested by the families of female students. However, students disputed this, stating their families were aware of the male teaching staff prior to enrollment and support the protests.

Students expressed concern that the sudden loss of academic supervisors complicates their studies, noting that many are currently tied to research and graduation projects overseen by the removed professors. They argued that the male instructors' familiarity with their specific academic strengths and weaknesses makes replacement difficult. During the protests, students reported that university administrators refused to discuss their concerns and mocked the demonstrations. On social media, some commentators accused the protesting women of attempting to keep male professors to “establish immoral relationships with them”.

Huda, a 22-year-old student, reported that when students attempted to demonstrate, the university president, Rahi al-Yasiri, blocked their path with bodyguards. Huda alleged that the bodyguards mocked the students and that al-Yasiri ordered them to take photographs of the protesters' faces in an attempt to intimidate and punish them later. When students questioned the logic of the policy by comparing it to doctors who treat both men and women, Huda said al-Yasiri replied: “Even if you hit your heads against the wall, I will not bring back the professors.”

cards.headline: Rutgers engineers develop fast noninvasive brain-computer communication system

pages.text: Engineers at Rutgers University have developed ChatBCI-Assist, a noninvasive brain-computer communication interface that uses artificial intelligence (AI) to translate brain activity into words and phrases at record-level speeds. The system allows users to reproduce sentences nearly twice as fast as a conventional, dictionary-based, predictive approach. Unlike systems that require reproducing every word precisely, this interface enables intent-based communication, where users select AI-generated phrases to convey their intended meaning. This technology could make communication considerably faster and less tiring for people with severe movement and speech impairments, such as those with advanced amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), a progressive disease that attacks nerve cells controlling muscles throughout the body.

The research was led by Laleh Najafizadeh, a professor in the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering at Rutgers School of Engineering and director of the university’s Integrated Systems and NeuroImaging Laboratory. The work was co-led by postdoctoral associate Weinan Wang. First author Jiazhen Hong, who earned a doctoral degree from Rutgers, carried out the work alongside graduate student Pradyumna Rao. The findings were published in IEEE Transactions on Biomedical Engineering. While the system has so far been evaluated only with healthy participants, clinical testing with individuals living with ALS is in the planning stages. Najafizadeh is collaborating with Shan Chen, a physician-scientist and medical director of the ALS Multidisciplinary Clinic at Rutgers Robert Wood Johnson Medical School and Robert Wood Johnson University Hospital.

cards.headline: Man on Canada's most wanted list arrested in Winnipeg for 2020 Bolton homicide

pages.text: Filmon Fesshaghirgis, 28, of London, Ontario, was arrested in Winnipeg by the RCMP and Winnipeg Police Service at approximately 4:10 p.m., according to the Ontario Provincial Police (OPP). Fesshaghirgis, who was ranked number 14 on a list of Canada's 25 most wanted fugitives, faces charges of first-degree murder, attempted murder, and conspiracy to commit murder. The OPP is making arrangements to return him to Ontario.

Police say Fesshaghirgis was wanted on a Canada-wide warrant related to two shooting incidents in the Greater Toronto Area. On Nov. 12, 2020, York Regional Police responded to a shooting at a business on Steeles Avenue W. in Vaughan, which left one person injured and hospitalized. On Jan. 18, 2021, Caledon OPP officers responded to a shooting at a home on Harvest Moon Drive in Bolton, Ontario, where two people suffered gunshot wounds. One of those victims was the individual injured in the Vaughan incident, and the second victim, 65-year-old Giovanni Costa of Bolton, was found dead at the scene.

cards.headline: Ancient 'supermountains' comparable in size to the Himalayas discovered beneath Antarctica

pages.text: An international team of scientists has identified the roots of a previously unknown system of ancient mountain ranges, referred to as 'supermountains,' buried beneath Antarctica's ice sheet. The mountain chains, which are comparable in size to the Himalayas, formed between 650 and 450 million years ago during the assembly of the Gondwana supercontinent. Researchers from the Australian National University (ANU) and Germany's GFZ Research Centre for Geosciences published their findings in the journal Earth and Planetary Science Letters. The scientists describe the formation of these ranges, caused by Antarctica colliding with India and Africa, as the largest mountain-building event to have affected the continent.

Because more than 99.5 per cent of Antarctica is covered by a thick ice sheet, the researchers could not study the rocks directly. Instead, the team analyzed sediments obtained from ocean drilling along the continental margin, examining 1,712 tiny mineral grains known as zircon crystals. These crystals allowed the experts to determine the age and chemical composition of the original rocks and infer the geological processes that created them, revealing the deeply buried, eroded roots of the former mountain ranges.

The discovery may offer an explanation for the evolution of life on Earth. Ian Campbell, an emeritus professor at ANU and co-author of the study, stated that the rapid erosion of these mountains played a key role in biological development. The weathering of the rocks delivered large quantities of nutrients to the oceans, lowered atmospheric carbon dioxide levels, and increased oxygen concentrations. According to Campbell, these conditions facilitated the appearance of the first organisms with hard skeletons 539 million years ago and contributed to the Cambrian explosion, a sudden increase in animal diversity.

cards.headline: CERN physicists find evidence of particle decay occurring once in every 10 billion beauty particles

pages.text: Physicists at CERN have found evidence of an extraordinarily rare particle decay after more than 40 years of searching. The process, known as 'Bd to mu mu', occurs approximately once in every 10 billion beauty particles. This finding comes from the upgraded LHCb experiment at CERN's Large Hadron Collider (LHC). Researchers at the University of Manchester contributed to the international effort by providing advanced technology used to make the measurement possible. The evidence has a statistical significance of 3.2 sigma, which is strong enough to qualify as evidence, though physicists require additional data before they can officially declare a discovery.

The detection of this decay provides a way to test the Standard Model, the primary scientific framework used to describe fundamental particles and their interactions. By studying this rare decay in detail, researchers aim to find clues regarding physics beyond current understanding, potentially revealing unknown particles and forces of nature. The LHCb experiment focuses on studying particles containing beauty quarks, which are heavier relatives of the up and down quarks that constitute much of the ordinary matter in the universe. These beauty quarks are produced in enormous numbers when particles collide inside the Large Hadron Collider.

cards.headline: Diesel leak into Skeena River following CN Rail derailment in northwest B.C.

pages.text: A CN Rail train derailed in northwest British Columbia, leaking diesel into the salmon-bearing Skeena River. The company stated that a suspected rockslide pushed a locomotive and several cars down an embankment and into the water, causing diesel from the locomotive to leak more than a kilometre downstream. Drone footage from the site shows a visible sheen traveling downstream. This is the second such incident in eight months, following a similar derailment during extreme weather this past March. CN Rail reported that it has repaired the track and traffic is running again.

The B.C. government stated that a containment boom and absorbent pads are in place and a surface water sampling plan has been drafted. The province has asked CN Rail to provide an estimate for the volume of diesel spilled, but the company has not yet shared that figure. Former NDP MP and former transport critic Taylor Bachrach, who lives in the region, called the derailments a “wake-up call,” noting that the railroad runs next to the Skeena River for hundreds of kilometres. Bachrach identified the river as highly important for salmon and stated that the consequences of a major disaster involving the shipment of dangerous goods along that line are “unthinkable.”

The incident reignites debate over shipping hazardous materials by rail in northwest B.C. The region's Port of Prince Rupert has become a key site for shipping energy products to overseas Asian markets. While efforts to build a pipeline to transport heavy crude oil to the North Coast have faced resistance due to environmental concerns, the transport of goods via rail remains a point of contention.

cards.headline: Experimental daily pill daraxonrasib shows potential to shrink or eliminate pancreatic cancer tumours in early trial

pages.text: An experimental daily pill called daraxonrasib has shown the ability to shrink or make tumours undetectable in some patients with advanced pancreatic cancer during a phase I/II trial. The drug, which is a KRAS inhibitor, works by locking onto and shutting off specific mutations that drive tumour growth in most pancreatic cancers. Researchers presented the findings at the EORTC-NCI-AACR Symposium on Molecular Targets and Cancer Therapeutics in Barcelona. Dr. Wungki Park, a gastrointestinal medical oncologist at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York, described the results as “the closest to cure,” noting he had not previously seen so many tumours disappear in patients whose cancer had spread to other parts of the body. There are hopes the treatment could work for dozens of other cancers that share similar mutations. During the trial, 61 participants with advanced pancreatic cancer that had spread to other organs were given daraxonrasib alongside chemotherapy. In this group, tumours stopped growing in 90 percent of participants, while just over 60 percent saw their tumours shrink or disappear. For approximately 8 percent of patients, scans showed no detectable cancer, a result the BBC reported occurred in about one in 12 patients.

While experts have described the findings as a major advance, doctors caution that the results do not mean the disease has been cured. Patients in the trial were followed for an average of 18 months, and while some did not see their cancer return during that period, researchers say longer studies are required to establish if the disease can enter remission and for how long. One year after starting treatment, 76.6 percent of patients were alive, compared to the 40-45 percent of patients who usually survive a year when given chemotherapy alone. Pancreatic cancer is difficult to treat; in the UK, it has the lowest survival rate of all common cancers, with half of all diagnosed patients dying within three months and only about 3 percent surviving five years once the disease spreads to other organs. Cancer Research UK called the findings “the biggest leap forward in decades” for patients, and Dr. Sam Godfrey of the charity told the BBC the results were “incredibly exciting” because the drug targets something previously considered difficult to treat.

cards.headline: Ottawa installs Canada's first permeable pavement roadway strip

pages.text: The City of Ottawa has completed the installation of a metre-wide strip of permeable pavement at the intersection of Anna Avenue and Crown Crescent, marking the first roadway of its kind in Canada. Located near the Central Experimental Farm, the installation follows an extremely wet summer that shattered regional rainfall records. Unlike standard pavement that directs runoff toward storm drains, this atypical asphalt acts like a sponge, absorbing rainfall and channeling it into a gravel-based drainage and storage system located underneath the surface.

The installation, which hugs the curb along Crown Crescent and runs along two-thirds of the street, serves as a pilot project. Researchers will monitor the system to determine how much stormwater it can hold and whether the approach can be scaled up. While the technology has been utilized in driveways and parking lots in other cities, local developer PurePave Technologies sought to implement it on a roadway in Ottawa. Taylor Davis, CEO of the Ottawa-based PurePave Technologies, noted that her own house flooded on Canada Day, and despite having 'enhanced' flood coverage, her insurer denied her claim.

Knoxdale-Merivale Councillor Sean Devine said he began conversations with PurePave Technologies in 2024 to explore adapting the technology for municipal use following a year of significant flooding. Devine stated that as the city and its population grow, more spaces are being paved with impermeable surfaces, which contributes to flooding.

cards.headline: Physicists use gravity to transmit message through brick wall

pages.text: Physicists at the University of Queensland in Australia have conducted a proof-of-concept experiment using gravity to transmit a message through a brick wall. By moving an elevator's counterweight to create changes in a gravitational field, researchers successfully sent the word “gravity” in binary code to a detector located approximately 70cm away in an adjacent men's bathroom. While the method is currently too slow for practical use, scientists describe it as a “practically unblockable wireless communication scheme” because, unlike electromagnetic signals used in modern wireless technology, gravitational signals cannot be screened out by ordinary materials like solid walls or tunnels.

The experiment utilized a sensitive detection device called a gravimeter, which was placed on the floor of a men's bathroom next to a 1950s-era elevator. To transmit data, researchers moved the elevator's 1.8-tonne counterweight between two different levels. The position of the counterweight represented either a 0 or a 1 in binary code. Using a transmission rate of one bit per minute, it took nearly an hour to send the single word “gravity” (1000111 1110010 1100001 1110110 1101001 1110100 1111001). The research was published in the journal Science Advances. Co-author Dr. Charles Woffinden, of the University of Queensland’s school of mathematics and physics, noted that the ability to bypass obstacles that typically block Wi-Fi or phone reception is a primary appeal of the concept. However, study co-author Prof. Matthew Davis stated that while the experiment was theoretically interesting, it is currently difficult to imagine how the technology could be practically useful.

cards.headline: Almost half of women in B.C. report experiencing intimate partner violence

pages.text: A Statistics Canada report released November 18, 2026, found that 47 per cent of women in British Columbia have reported experiencing intimate partner violence at least once since the age of 15. The study defines intimate partner violence as psychological, physical, and sexual abuse, ranging from name-calling and manipulation to physical and sexual assault. This figure, based on 2025 data, has held steady since a previous report examining 2018 data. The findings come from the 2025 Survey of Safety in Public and Private Spaces, which included over 46,500 respondents across Canada's 10 provinces via telephone and online administration.

Nationwide, 45.1 per cent of women reported experiencing intimate partner violence, an increase from 44 per cent. The study also found that more younger women, aged 15 to 24 years old, are reporting intimate partner violence across the country, with that specific figure rising to 58.5 per cent from 55.75 per cent. Angela Marie MacDougall, executive director of Battered Women's Support Services, suggested the uptick may result from an increased willingness to report compared to previous generations, noting that survivors in the past often did not report and instead had to deal with the abuse.

cards.headline: New study shows Wernicke’s area is responsible for language production

pages.text: A study published in Science on November 19, 2026, has challenged the long-held scientific understanding of how the brain produces language. For approximately 150 years, neuroscience has operated under the model that two distinct brain regions handle language: Wernicke’s area for listening and Broca’s area for speaking. This new discovery shows that Wernicke’s area is actually responsible for language production as well as speech perception, revealing a much more complex brain structure than previously understood.

The traditional model was based on 19th-century observations by physicians Carl Wernicke and Paul Broca, who studied patients with aphasia—a language disorder. By observing the effects of brain damage, Broca identified that patients who struggled to produce speech had damage to a specific region of the frontal lobe near the temple. This led to the textbook definition of two separate centers for language: Broca’s area for speech production and Wernicke’s area for speech perception. The new findings resolve a paradox originally identified by Wernicke himself by demonstrating the dual role of Wernicke's area in both perceiving and producing language.

John Jay Ngai, the director of the National Institutes of Health’s BRAIN Initiative, described the discovery as “an amazing achievement” of neuroscience during a press briefing at the annual meeting of the Society for Neuroscience. The findings suggest that the fundamental descriptions of language processing found in most textbooks will need to be rewritten.
